newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees growing leaks at radioactive waste dump.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees growing leaks at radioactive waste dump.

text.p: Radioactive leakage from a nuclear waste dump in the desert at Beatty, Nevada, has been increasing over the last five years, a U.S. Geological Survey scientist said on Monday.

"We do have enough of a history at this point to be able to say there's been a general increase in the tritium levels from 1992 to 1996," said William Alley, chief of the geological survey's office of groundwater.
Tritium is a radioactive form of hydrogen.

Environmentalists pointed to the findings to bolster their arguments for blocking a similar proposed dump in the Mojave Desert in Ward Valley, California, for low level radioactive waste from nuclear plants, labs and hospitals.

The Interior Department has delayed handing over the Ward Valley land to the state while it negotiates guidelines with California. The department wants to test whether radioactive material could seep from a dump into groundwater near the Colorado River, which is a key source of drinking water.
"The worsening conditions in Nevada provide ample proof that Ward Valley will leak, too," said Joseph Lyou of the Committee to Bridge the Gap, a group opposed to the project.
However, Alley said the increase in levels of tritium in the soil near the Nevada desert site did not necessarily indicate what might happen at Ward Valley.
"The data really aren't very useful for trying to say anything about Ward Valley," he said in an interview.
He said the tritium appeared to have percolated out from the site because liquid tritium was dumped into trenches that were left open for a year or more.

"Given that those are not the practices stated -- at least on paper -- for Ward Valley, there's really no way to make a comparison about what the practices at Ward Valley might result in," Alley said.
The Beatty dump, which closed in 1992, was run by U.S. Ecology, the same company that California has chosen to operate the Ward Valley dump.
The geological survey discovered the leakage from Beatty at a nearby research facility that was testing for atmospheric fallout from nuclear bomb tests in the 1960s.
They suspected tritium showing up in soil vapor and water samples had to be coming from Beatty because the levels were higher than would have been expected from atmospheric fallout.
